attribution: Adi Shankaracharya; generally accepted as authentic
author: shankara
period: Traditionally 8th century CE; scholars generally place Shankara in the 7th–8th centuries
summary: The oldest surviving complete commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, reading it as teaching liberation through knowledge of the Self.
whyRead: Shankara's commentary shaped how the Gita was read for centuries, and later commentators often define their positions against it. It is especially useful for seeing how Advaita handles the Gita's teaching on action.
questions: Does the Gita teach action or renunciation?
Can knowledge and action be combined?
Who is the Self that the Gita describes?

keyTeachings.title: The Gita's goal is knowledge
keyTeachings.text: Shankara holds that the Gita's ultimate teaching is liberation through knowledge of the Self as Brahman, preceded by renunciation.

keyTeachings.title: Against combining knowledge and action
keyTeachings.text: He argues against the view that knowledge and ritual action must be combined for liberation (jnana-karma-samuccaya); action purifies the mind and prepares one for knowledge.

keyTeachings.title: Karma yoga as preparation
keyTeachings.text: Action without attachment is valued as a discipline for those not yet ready for knowledge, purifying the mind.

structure.label: Introduction
structure.note: Frames the Gita's teaching as twofold: action and withdrawal

structure.label: Verse-by-verse commentary, with longer discussions at key verses such as 2.10–11

passages.about: Shankara's extended argument on knowledge and action
